common_name: Jackmanii Alba Clematis (White-Flowered Sport of Jackmanii, Group 3 Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Jackmanii Alba flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: A white-flowered sport of the classic 1862 hybrid Jackmanii, raised by the Jackman nursery in England, Jackmanii Alba opens semi-double, creamy white flowers with a faint greenish cast in its earliest flush, followed later in the season by smaller single white blooms with cream stamens. Like its purple parent it flowers entirely on the current year's growth from midsummer into early fall, so the whole vine should be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3). Its vigor, disease resistance, and tolerance of a wide range of soils make it as forgiving for beginners as the straight Jackmanii, just in a cooler color.

common_name: Lincoln Star Clematis (Rich Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with Deep Carmine Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Lincoln Star flowers on old wood in early summer, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2), with a lighter repeat bloom possible on new growth in late summer.

directions: Raised in England and widely grown since the mid-20th century, Lincoln Star bears large, rich carmine-pink flowers up to 7 inches across with a darker pink central bar and conspicuous red anthers. The main flush opens in early summer on the previous year's growth, often followed by a lighter repeat bloom on new wood into late summer. Its bright, saturated color and reliable performance have earned it a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit and made it a long-standing favorite for a sunny obelisk or fence.

common_name: Ken Donson Clematis (Deep Mid-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Ken Donson flowers on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2).

directions: An English large-flowered hybrid, Ken Donson produces rounded, deep mid-blue flowers up to 8 inches across with golden-yellow stamens, among the largest blooms of any blue clematis cultivar. Flowering opens in late spring on the previous year's growth, with a lighter second flush on new growth in late summer, so pruning should stay light and be done right after the main bloom (Group 2). Its exceptional flower size and clear blue color have kept it popular for training up a pillar or trellis where individual blooms can be seen up close.

common_name: Mrs. N. Thompson Clematis (Compact Violet-Purple Large-Flowered Clematis with Red Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Mrs. N. Thompson flowers on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2).

directions: Raised by the English nursery Pennell & Sons, Mrs. N. Thompson bears rich violet-purple flowers with a bold scarlet-red central bar down each tepal, a strongly bicolor pattern that softens as the bloom ages. It flowers on the previous year's growth from late spring into early summer, then again more lightly on new growth, so pruning should be light and done just after the first flush (Group 2). Its naturally compact, restrained habit compared to more rampant large-flowered hybrids makes it one of the better clematis choices for a large container or a small trellis.

common_name: Margot Koster Clematis (Dusky Pink Nodding Viticella Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Margot Koster is a viticella-type clematis that blooms on new growth and can be cut back hard each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Raised by the Koster nursery in the Netherlands, Margot Koster bears small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers in a dusky mauve-pink with tepals that recurve sharply at the tips as the bloom matures. Like other viticella cultivars it flowers prolifically on the current season's growth from midsummer into early fall, so the entire vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3). Its soft, unusual coloring and reliable, easy pruning regime make it a favorite for scrambling through a spent early-summer shrub or climbing rose.

common_name: Emilia Plater Clematis (Azure-Blue Nodding Late-Season Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Emilia Plater flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Bred in Poland by the noted clematis hybridizer Brother Stefan Franczak and named for the 19th-century Polish-Lithuanian noblewoman, Emilia Plater bears nodding, azure to lavender-blue flowers with narrow, gently twisted tepals. It flowers on the current season's growth from midsummer into early fall, so the whole vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3). Its graceful, informal flower form and long bloom season make it a good companion for climbing roses and other midsummer-blooming shrubs.

common_name: Madame Édouard André Clematis (Velvety Crimson-Red Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Madame Édouard André flowers on new growth, so cut the whole vine back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3).

directions: Introduced in France in 1893, Madame Édouard André bears velvety, deep crimson-red flowers with cream-yellow stamens, one of the oldest true red-toned large-flowered clematis still in general cultivation. It flowers abundantly on the current season's growth from early summer into fall, so the whole vine can be cut back hard to about a foot from the ground each late winter (Group 3). Its rich color, long bloom season, and tolerance of hard annual pruning have kept it a mainstay of red-flowered clematis for well over a century.

common_name: Asao Clematis (Deep Pink Large-Flowered Clematis with White Central Bar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Asao flowers on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2).

directions: Bred in Japan by Kaneko and introduced in the 1970s, Asao bears large, deep carmine-pink flowers with a paler, near-white central bar down each tepal and a mound of cream stamens at the center. It flowers on the previous year's growth in late spring to early summer, followed by a lighter repeat flush on new growth later in the season, so pruning should be light and done right after the main bloom (Group 2). Its strong bicolor pattern and free-flowering habit have made it a popular large-flowered cultivar in North American nurseries.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Fujimusume flowers on old wood in late spring, so prune only lightly right after the main flush (Group 2).

directions: A Japanese-bred cultivar whose name translates roughly as 'wisteria maiden,' Fujimusume produces large, clear lavender-blue flowers with pointed, slightly overlapping tepals and cream-yellow stamens, considered one of the truest blues among large-flowered hybrids. It flowers on the previous year's growth in late spring, with a lighter repeat bloom on new growth in late summer, so pruning should stay light and be timed just after the first flush (Group 2). Its exceptionally clear blue color makes it a popular companion for white or yellow climbing roses.

common_name: Princess Kate Clematis (Deep Purple-Blue Compact Viticella-Type Clematis)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface, keeping roots cool and shaded; Princess Kate flowers on both old and new wood, so light pruning (Group 2) preserves the earliest flush while still allowing a strong repeat bloom.

directions: Part of the Raymond Evison Boulevard Collection bred for compact growth, Princess Kate bears deep purple-blue flowers with a paler central bar and contrasting cream stamens on a naturally restrained vine well suited to patio containers. It flowers over an unusually long season from early summer into fall on both old and new growth, so light pruning (Group 2) preserves the earliest flush while still allowing strong repeat bloom. Its compact habit and extended flowering period have made it a popular choice for gardeners without room for a full-sized clematis.
